summary: For 11–12 year-olds (KS3 / NGSS MS), replace everyday energy WORDS with a disciplined MODEL: a small set of quantifiable energy STORES (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) connected by a small set of transfer PATHWAYS (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation). The core teaching moves are: (1) trace ONE process at a time from its start stores to its end stores — do not build long chains, naming the pathway(s) between; and (2) keep STORE (a quantity at an instant) categorically distinct from PATHWAY (a process over time), with the '-ing' naming signalling processes. The highest-value KS3 correction is that electric current, light and sound are PATHWAYS, not stores. Start→end 'bar charts' (how full is each store before and after?) make the model concrete; attaching joules early previews energy as a bookkeeping quantity.
misconceptions: Treating 'electrical energy', 'light energy' or 'sound energy' as STORES rather than pathways/processes — the central KS3 error the stores-and-pathways model is designed to fix.
Building long energy chains and 'renaming' energy at every intermediate step instead of focusing on the start and end stores.
Confusing a store (quantifiable at an instant) with a pathway (a process over time) — e.g. calling 'heating' a store, or 'thermal' a process.
Thinking energy is a tangible substance/fluid that physically flows, rather than an abstract quantity tracked between stores.
Believing only moving things have energy, missing stored (potential) energy in raised, stretched, chemical or thermal stores.
Calling the thermal store 'heat' — heat is a process (heating), not the way energy is stored.

activities.title: Energy tracker: predict and trace the start and end stores of one process
steps: Pick a familiar process one at a time: a falling ball, a torch switched on, a kettle heating, a bow firing an arrow, a car braking.
Before running it, PREDICT which store empties and which fills, and name the pathway (or pathways) between them (e.g. mechanical working; electrical working; heating by radiation).
Represent the start and end as energy bar charts: one bar per store, with fill level showing how much energy is in each at the START snapshot and at the END snapshot.
Check your prediction against the recomputed end snapshot and name where the energy ends up (often the thermal store of the surroundings).

Worked single-process examples to study: falling ball (gravitational store → kinetic store, by mechanical working); electric kettle (energy transferred by electrical working from the mains supply into the thermal store of the water and kettle — one unchained process; the store that empties is outside the kettle, e.g. at the power station, so the bar chart shows energy coming in rather than a kettle store emptying); torch (chemical store of the battery → [electrical working, then heating by radiation] → thermal store of the surroundings).
activities.insight: Energy can be tracked as a quantity that moves between a small set of stores along named pathways; focusing on just the start and end stores of a single process makes conservation and relocation visible without renaming energy at every intermediate step.

activities.title: Sort it: STORE or PATHWAY?
steps: Sort cards into two bins — STORES (kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical, nuclear, magnetic/electrostatic) and PATHWAYS (mechanical working, electrical working, heating by particles, heating by radiation).
Place the tricky cards: electric current, light and sound — these go in the PATHWAY bin, because they describe how energy is carried, not where it sits.

For each of the four named pathway cards, explain that its 'working/heating' naming marks it as a process happening over time (electric current, light and sound lack this ending but still describe transfers: electrical working, radiation and mechanical working by vibrations); for each store card, explain it is something you could quantify at an instant.
Catch and correct the distractor claim: 'The torch stores electrical energy and light energy, which are two of the energy stores.' State why that is wrong.
activities.insight: Stores (quantifiable snapshots) and pathways (processes over time) are different categories; 'electrical', 'light' and 'sound' name transfers, not storage — the central KS3 error the model fixes.

activities.title: Store-and-pathway reference anchor
steps: Study a labelled reference: each store with one real-world example (e.g. raised object = gravitational; stretched bow = elastic; hot water = thermal; battery = chemical) and the note that each store is something you could quantify.
Study the four pathways listed as arrows/processes, each marked as 'a process, over time'.
Examine a fixed worked example laid out side by side: torch — chemical store → [electrical working + heating by radiation] → thermal store of the surroundings.
Use the two-category layout (stores on one side, pathways on the other) to self-check before and during the tracing task.
activities.insight: Seeing the two categories side by side, with examples, pre-empts the store/pathway confusion and gives a glossary learners can return to while tracing.

activities.title: Optional numbers mode: energy as a bookkeeping quantity
steps: Re-run a traced process whose stores are all included (e.g. falling ball, car braking) with joule values attached to each store bar; for a mains device such as a kettle, record the joules supplied by electrical working from outside as an input, rather than expecting a store inside the kettle to empty.
Check that the total across all stores is accounted for before and after the process — what leaves one store appears in another.

State in words that, when every store involved (including the surroundings and any energy supplied from outside) is counted, the total energy has the same value before and after the change, even though it has moved between stores and often ended in the thermal store of the surroundings.
activities.insight: Energy reads as a calculable, conserved bookkeeping quantity rather than a vague essence; the total is conserved while stores fill and empty.

checkQuestion: A battery-powered torch is switched on and shines. Name the energy STORE it starts in and the store it ends up in, and name the PATHWAY that carries the energy between them. Someone writes 'chemical energy turns into light energy and electrical energy.' What's wrong with calling light and electrical 'stores'?
checkAnswer: It starts in the chemical store (battery) and ends mostly in the thermal store of the surroundings (the light is absorbed and warms things). The pathways are electrical working (battery to bulb) then radiation and heating. 'Electrical', 'light' and 'sound' are PATHWAYS — ways energy is carried between stores — not stores it sits in; only kinetic, gravitational, elastic, thermal, chemical and nuclear are stores.
